sources.news_title: Rep. Jordan, Sen. Thune wins votes to lead GOP minority after midterms blowout
sources.text:
Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, decisively won a closed-door vote to lead the Republican minority in the House of Representatives while Sen. John Thune was r-elected to lead the GOP caucus in the next Congress after the party suffered sweeping losses in the midterm elections.
Right-wing firebrand Jordan beat Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., by a healthy 106-73 margin in a secret-ballot election that came after House Speaker Mike Johnson announced he would step down in light of the party’s defeat last week.
Jordan, 62, who relishes playing political hardball, will likely be a combative Republican foil to presumptive incoming House Speaker Rep. Hakeem Jeffries and may seek to rebuild the GOP’s foundation in the House after the party lost close to 50 seats in one of the worst beat-downs in recent history.
“I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” he wrote to his Republican colleagues in a pitch for his candidacy. “Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections.”
Thune was elected by acclamation at a closed-door meeting. Some GOP senators unsuccessfully pushed for the vote to be delayed to consider the implications of the midterms wipeout, in which Democrats flipped at least seven seats, with two still uncalled but leaning left.
Jordan may have had the edge over Scalise because the Louisiana lawmaker was Johnson’s top lieutenant for the past four years and the sitting leadership team must shoulder a share of the blame for the midterms debacle.
By picking Jordan, the shrunken GOP House caucus is signaling they want to take a pugnacious approach to dealing with ascendant Democrats in Congress. Even though he’s also a staunch conservative, Scalise was seen as being more likely to be willing to cut deals with the other side when possible.
The House Speaker will only be elected when the new Congress is seated in January. Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to win the 218 votes he needs to win the gavel because Democrats will hold about 260 seats.
Both Jordan and Scalise lost prior bids for House Speaker during a chaotic period in 2023 after Rep. Kevin McCarthy was stripped of the gavel by Republican hard-liners.
Jordan, who has served as chair of the House Judiciary Committee, has warned GOP colleagues to brace themselves for an aggressive Democratic push to investigate President Trump’s administration and to hobble his chances of winning any policy wins during his final two years in office.
Jordan will also face the difficult task of clawing back a chunk of the nearly 50 seats Democrats won in the midterms as soon as 2028.
Sen. Chuck Schumer is the favorite to retain his position as Senate Democratic leader although several senators have said they oppose his bid.

sources.news_title: House Republicans elect Jim Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress
sources.text:
House Republicans on Tuesday elected Jim Jordan as minority leader for the next Congress, beating House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, according to multiple sources.
Jordan got 106 votes to Scalise’s 73 votes, the sources said.
As of Tuesday, House Democrats hold a 254-166 margin over Republicans going into the 120th Congress with 15 races still undecided.
In the Senate, Sen. John Thune of South Dakota will remain as the party’s leader despite some in his conference delaying the vote while they discussed the results of the midterm elections and the party’s path forward.
Jordan has led Republicans at the Oversight and Judiciary committees, where his hardline approach and reputation as an ardent defender of President Donald Trump have made him a popular cable TV news guest.
First elected in 2007, Jordan is a two-time NCAA champion wrestler.
Scalise, first elected in 2008, was critically injured during a shooting at practice for the congressional baseball game in 2017. He’s served at the Republican leadership table for more than a decade — including as the GOP’s No. 2 leader since 2023. Scalise is also in remission from multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, which he was treated for in late 2023, taking a six-week absence to undergo chemotherapy.
Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota, the current majority whip, was elected to serve as GOP minority whip, beating a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger. And Rep. Lisa McClain of Michigan was elected to serve as GOP conference chair — the No. 3 position among House Republicans in the minority — according to multiple sources. She beat challenges from Rep. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Rep. Greg Steube of Florida.
Jordan and Scalise, along with Emmer, ran for speaker in 2023 when then-Speaker Kevin McCarthy was ousted after a revolt from a small group of far-right Republicans.
Speaker Mike Johnson was elected after a chaotic battle that shut the conference down for three weeks.
Johnson announced last week that he wouldn’t stand for election as minority leader, giving the GOP conference an opportunity to pick up the pieces of their shattered majority after the midterm elections by choosing fresh leadership or run it back with Johnson’s top two deputies, Scalise and Emmer.
Senate leadership elections
Meanwhile, Senate Republicans on Tuesday afternoon approved Thune by acclimation to remain the conference’s leader in the minority after “family” discussions about the best path forward for the party.
Senate Republicans gathered Tuesday morning for what was scheduled to be their leadership elections, but rather than holding votes, they instead engaged in what was described as a “frank” discussion about how Republicans ought to respond in the wake of last week’s bruising midterm elections that left Republicans down at least seven Senate seats with two races yet to be decided.
Though some Republicans said they were unsure whether they wanted to stick with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota as their leader following voter backlash in the midterms, no one else emerged as a potential challenger.
In addition to Thune, the caucus re-elected the rest of its previous leadership: Sen. John Barrasso will remain as Senate GOP whip and Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas will remain Republican Conference chair.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, who was unopposed, was elected chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the Republican conference’s campaign operation, replacing South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott.
In a post on X, Thune said he “appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today,” and that the Republican team remains “united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left liberal agenda.”
In a letter sent Monday obtained by ABC News, dozens of Republican National Committee members called for Republicans to delay leadership elections in both the House and the Senate for 30 days to give the party time to evaluate its losses and how leadership candidates plan to move the party forward.
“There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated. These devastating losses are historic, and they threaten to undo all the work of the last 10 years,” the letter addressed to Congressional Republicans reads.
“Members deserve to understand what went wrong and hear how those seeking leadership intend to address those failures before casting their votes. That assessment should inform the choice of leadership. Holding elections first gets that backward.”

sources.news_title: Jordan wins House GOP leader race as Senate Republicans weigh keeping Thune
sources.text:
Republicans will have a new leader in the House and a familiar one in the Senate as they prepare for their new role in the minority.
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio won the race Tuesday to serve as House Republican leader. Also Tuesday, Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader after a tense day of discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Jordan, who serves as chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, defeated Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana in a secret ballot election of Republicans who will serve in the next Congress. The vote was 106-73.
House Speaker Mike Johnson did not seek reelection to his leadership post.
Jordan, 62, is a co-founder of the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election debacle and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
Jordan as minority leader will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office. Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms.
Jordan warned of the coming Democratic efforts on oversight, with numerous investigations of the Trump administration expected.
“Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections,” Jordan said, a nod to his pugnacious reputation in committee hearings.
Trump said he was staying out of the race.
Scalise and Jordan had faced off before, both running to serve as House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the job a little more than three years ago. Neither was able to rally the support necessary to secure the position, which eventually went to Mike Johnson, who is stepping aside from the leadership in the new Congress.
Scalise, 61, has held key GOP leadership positions going back to 2014, serving as party whip and then as majority leader. In 2017, he was critically wounded when a gunman opened fire at a baseball practice where several Republican lawmakers and staffers were preparing for an annual charity baseball game against Democrats. In 2023, he was stricken with multiple myeloma, a blood cancer that was successfully treated.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings on Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted to proceed, said Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson, who had pushed to postpone. He walked out of the room as the voting began.
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said after the first meeting that “we want to be thoughtful and do the right thing."
Justice said there was a "legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn't cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
The angst — and the indecision — comes as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.
But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.

sources.news_title: Jim Jordan selected to lead GOP minority when new U.S. House convenes in January
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives have chosen a fighter to lead them into their new status as the minority party.
Rep. Jim Jordan, whose 4th District in Ohio now includes parts of Richland and Delaware counties, was selected Tuesday to be the party’s leader when the 120th Congress takes office in January.
The 62-year-old former high school and collegiate wrestler defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., a close ally to outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to become minority leader.
The vote, held behind closed doors and by secret ballot, was 106-73, according to two lawmakers in the room in a story published by NBC News.
In his announcement seeking the GOP leadership position, Jordan warned of the coming Democratic efforts on oversight, with numerous investigations of the Trump administration expected.
“Our job cannot be merely to spotlight how radical this new Democratic Party is — offense, not defense, wins elections,” Jordan said, a nod to his reputation in committee hearings.
“I am battle-tested on the oversight front and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” he wrote to his colleagues after a national “blue wave” a week ago handed Democrats control of the next House and Senate.
Jordan, first elected to Congress in 2006, helped launch the conservative House Freedom Caucus in 2015 and served as its first chairman.
His candidacy appealed to those looking for new leadership in the wake of last week’s election losses and to those who like his hard-hitting political style.
“Jordan as minority leader will inherit a historically small House Republican conference that is only beginning to grapple with its loss of power as President Donald Trump serves out his final two years in office,” according to a story published by the Associated Press.
“Leading the party back to the House majority in 2028 is sure to be a stiff climb, given the scope of Democratic victories in the midterms.”
Jordan was re-elected in the 4th District on Nov. 3, earning almost 65 percent of the votes cast. He received 62.5 percent of the votes in Richland County and 49.6 percent of the votes in Delaware County.
As Jordan prepares to lead House Republicans, he will face the challenge of steering a narrower conference while balancing aggressive oversight against legislative dealmaking in a divided capital.
Before the election, Jordan sat down with Richland Source in Mansfield, offering a candid look into his political philosophy, his combative style in congressional hearings and the working-class roots that guide him.
In the interview, Jordan made no apologies for his reputation as one of Capitol Hill’s most relentless cross-examiners, drawing a direct parallel between high-stakes hearings and his athletic background as an NCAA champion wrestler.
“When it comes to the job … I really like when I get the chance to cross-examine a witness in a hearing, particularly when I think that witness hasn’t been square with the people I get the privilege of serving,” Jordan said.
“When you get a chance to cross-examine them, that’s as close to wrestling as you can get — close to competition as you can get,” said Jordan, who has chaired the House Judiciary Committee.
Having spearheaded high-profile investigations into the Biden administration, the Justice Department, and special counsel Jack Smith, Jordan reflected on what he views as a pattern in congressional oversight:
“The only thing we get wrong when we start these investigations… is it’s always worse than we thought. It always turns out the government did — you’re like, ‘They did what?’ We thought they were doing this, but they went past that.”
Despite his partisan clashes, Jordan pushed back against the idea that political polarization prevents mutual respect. He pointed specifically to his working relationship with Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), his Democratic counterpart on the Judiciary Committee.
“Jamie Raskin, my counterpart on Judiciary — I mean, he is a lefty, completely. We disagree on a lot, a lot of things. On most things,” Jordan said. “Even though he’s got Trump Derangement Syndrome worse than any human being I’ve ever been around, I feel like you still should [get along], and every once in a while you’ll find some areas where you can work together.”
Jordan highlighted civil liberties, Fourth Amendment privacy, and press protection as key areas of rare bipartisan alignment, citing joint efforts on press shield legislation and the Non-Disclosure Order (NDO) Fairness Act to curb government surveillance of citizens’ phone and digital records.
“It’s supposed to be about having robust debate, not just being mad at someone because they’re a different politics,” he added, decrying the rise in personal vitriol. “You don’t have to agree with me, but I would never yell at you just because I disagree with your politics.”
When asked how citizens should navigate misinformation and disinformation, Jordan warned sharply against government intervention and social media censorship.
“I get nervous when the government’s making that distinction — making that call. That’s when you get censorship,” Jordan said. “I trust the American people to dig through it much more than I trust the government to label it and censor it. Someone can say something crazy, ridiculous, wrong… and the way to combat that is not to stop it, but to have people say something that’s right, and correct, and true.”
Reflecting on his upbringing, Jordan credited his worldview to his parents and the blue-collar work ethic instilled during his youth in Ohio.
“My dad was a union worker at GM in Dayton, and my mom cleaned houses, and they busted their tail,” Jordan said.
“You just learned to work… My brother and I had a lawn mowing business. You’d do the stuff around the house, mow two or three lawns, come back home and practice at night because you were training in summer wrestling to get ready for the high school season. And you just worked all the time. That’s just an American thing, too. Americans work,” Jordan said.
U.S. Rep. Troy Balderson, whose 12th District in Ohio includes Knox County and part of Delaware County, praised the party’s decision.
“Jim is a dedicated public servant and proud Ohioan who is committed to protecting our freedoms and keeping America on the path to prosperity,” Balderson said in an email Tuesday afternoon.
“He knows our nation’s best days are yet to come and is the leader we need to stand firm on common-sense conservative principles that will keep our country strong and secure,” said Balderson, who was re-elected Nov. 3.
“Jim’s motto is ‘do what you say you’re going to do.’ I look forward to doing exactly that and delivering results for Ohio and the American people,” Balderson said.

The secret-ballot election followed days of internal discussions about the party’s future after Democrats captured control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 elections.
Jordan, 62, will officially become House minority leader when the 120th Congress convenes on January 3, 2027. He will replace outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, who announced last week that he would not seek another leadership position after Republicans lost their House majority.
The leadership change represents a significant shift for House Republicans, who are preparing to operate with substantially fewer members and reduced legislative authority. Jordan will be responsible for organizing the Republican conference, developing its political strategy, and coordinating its response to the incoming Democratic majority.
The Ohio Republican has built his congressional career around aggressive oversight, constitutional disputes, and confrontations with Democratic administrations. As chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, he has frequently challenged Democratic officials over federal law enforcement, immigration policy, and the conduct of executive branch agencies.
Jordan’s close relationship with President Trump has also made him one of the administration’s most recognizable defenders in Congress. He played a prominent role in opposing previous impeachment efforts against Trump and has repeatedly challenged investigations targeting the president.
His election signals that House Republicans are preparing for a confrontational period under Democratic leadership rather than adopting a more conciliatory approach following their election losses.
In a letter to Republican colleagues announcing his candidacy, Jordan argued that the party needed a clear strategy for operating in the minority. He warned that Republicans could not afford to remain reactive while Democrats pursued their legislative and investigative priorities.
Jordan emphasized that his experience leading congressional investigations would help Republicans respond to Democratic oversight efforts targeting the Trump administration.
He described himself as battle-tested and familiar with the political tactics Democrats have used in previous congressional confrontations. Jordan argued that the Republican conference needed to remain unified, communicate effectively, and prepare for the challenges ahead.
The Ohio congressman also stressed that Republicans must do more than criticize Democratic policies. He called for a proactive strategy that would allow the party to advance its own priorities and prepare for future elections.
His message resonated with enough Republican lawmakers to defeat Scalise, who had served in senior House leadership positions for more than a decade.
Scalise, 61, entered the contest emphasizing his experience managing legislation, coordinating Republican members, and raising money for congressional campaigns. He argued that his established relationships and leadership record would help the party navigate its transition into the minority.
The Louisiana Republican has held prominent leadership roles since 2014, serving as House majority whip, minority whip, and majority leader. He also helped guide major Republican legislation through Congress during President Trump’s second administration.
In his campaign for minority leader, Scalise highlighted his fundraising efforts during the midterm election cycle and argued that Republicans needed experienced leadership to rebuild their congressional presence.
However, Jordan’s emphasis on aggressive opposition and his record of conducting investigations proved decisive in the leadership election.
The contest revived a rivalry between the two Republicans that began during the chaotic House speaker election in October 2023.
Following the removal of Speaker Kevin McCarthy, Scalise initially secured the Republican nomination for speaker but withdrew after failing to obtain enough support to win a House floor vote.

Three years later, Republicans have turned to Jordan as they prepare for a dramatically different political environment.

Johnson will remain in Congress as a representative from Louisiana but will no longer lead House Republicans when the new session begins.

His election gives Republicans a leader with extensive experience in congressional investigations and a longstanding relationship with President Trump at a time when the administration is preparing for heightened scrutiny.

The Ohio Republican’s immediate challenge will be preparing his conference for the transition in January while helping Republicans respond to the political consequences of their election losses.

Ohio Congressman Jim Jordan to succeed Mike Johnson as GOP House minority leader, promising unity and a robust opposition.
Washington, DC – One week after losing their majority in midterm elections in the United States, Republicans in the US House of Representatives have chosen Congressman Jim Jordan as their new minority leader.
In a secret ballot vote held on Tuesday, the Ohio lawmaker, who was first elected to the US Congress in 2007, won the support of his fellow party members to succeed Mike Johnson as the chamber’s top Republican.
The high-stakes decision comes as Republicans try to chart a path forward after a bruising midterm defeat in which Democrats flipped at least 40 seats nationwide.
Jordan had been vying with current House Majority Leader Steve Scalise for the role, which will carry a host of responsibilities as Republicans prepare to message against at least two years of Democrat-led investigations into US President Donald Trump’s administration and pick a 2028 presidential nominee.
In a reported letter to his fellow Republicans before Tuesday’s vote, Jordan described himself as a “battle-tested” leader who was ready to take on those challenges.
“I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics”, he wrote. “We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting”.
Jordan, a top Trump ally, has been an influential voice in the Republican caucus. He cofounded the conservative House Freedom Caucus, which has frustrated many former and current Republican leaders and thwarted party-backed legislation.
The group’s chairman, Republican Congressman Andy Harris, congratulated Jordan after the vote, calling him “a fierce fighter, uniter, principled conservative, and relentless advocate for the American people”.
“Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats”, Harris said in a statement.
As the current chairman of the House Judiciary Committee, Jordan has used his power to look into what he has argued is the weaponisation of government against Trump. He has led the panel’s investigations into former US Special Counsel Jack Smith and Fulton County, Georgia, District Attorney Fani Willis, who both have unsuccessfully prosecuted the president.
Jordan’s allies on the panel were quick to praise his selection.
“Jim is a fighter and a convicted conservative,” Republican Congressman Brandon Gill wrote on social media. “He’s the original congressional brawler and is exactly what our Conference needs to lead us back to the majority”.

He has been a staunch defender of US military aid to Israel, as well as the US and Israel’s war on Iran.
Jordan, who once worked as an assistant wrestling coach at Ohio State University, had faced allegations that he had knowledge of sexual abuse of student-athletes by the team’s physician, Dr Richard Strauss, from 1978 to 1998. Jordan has denied the allegations.
He previously made a short-lived bid for US House speaker after Kevin McCarthy was ousted from the role in 2023.
Since then, Jordan has taken a less adversarial approach and aligned himself with Johnson and other members of the current House Republican leadership.
Before Jordan’s victory was sealed, McCarthy went on a podcast after last week’s midterm results to offer some advice to the future leader of the US House Republican conference.
“You can’t just play it day by day”, he told his former aides on Glory, Grief and the Gavel. “You’ve got to have a strategy, because it’ll knock the Democrats off base”.
McCarthy added: “You better have an acknowledgement of what transpired in this last election. Because you got to tell the American people I heard you and it’s going to take time to earn your trust again.”

sources.text:
House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio as their leader for the next Congress on Tuesday, choosing the Judiciary Committee chairman over Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana a week after Democrats won control of both chambers. The vote in a closed-door conference meeting was 106 to 73, according to people in the room. Jordan will become minority leader when the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3, replacing Speaker Mike Johnson at the top of the Republican conference.
Johnson had announced that he would not seek the minority leader's post and would step down from leadership, a decision that opened a two-way race between his closest deputy and one of the conference's best-known conservatives.
Jordan, 62, co-founded the House Freedom Caucus and served as its first chairman. He has led the Judiciary Committee for the past four years. In his pitch to colleagues, he argued that he is the Republican best positioned to counter Democratic investigations of the Trump administration and its allies, describing himself as "battle-tested on the oversight front" and familiar with the Democrats' playbook. He campaigned extensively for House Republican candidates this year, which some colleagues read as groundwork for a leadership run.
Scalise, a close Johnson ally who has been the conference's second-ranking member, told colleagues he could unify the party's factions against the incoming Democratic majority. After a candidate forum on Tuesday morning, he said the difference between the two men was that he had a proven record. Seventy-three members sided with him.
The contest was a rematch of sorts. After Kevin McCarthy was removed as speaker in October 2023, both Scalise and Jordan sought the gavel, and neither could assemble the votes needed on the House floor. Republicans eventually turned to Johnson, who had not been part of the fight. Tuesday's election was different in one important respect: it required only a majority of Republicans voting in conference, not a majority of the full House.
The vote went ahead over objections from parts of the party. More than 30 members of the Republican National Committee had asked House and Senate leaders to delay leadership elections for at least a month, arguing that the party needed time to absorb the results. House Republicans declined. Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland was among the members who backed Jordan publicly before the vote.
Senate Republicans took longer. Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota was reelected as the conference's leader on Tuesday, but only after a closed-door meeting that stretched through the day as a group of his colleagues pressed for a postponement. The conference paused its election at one point before returning to choose him. He will serve as minority leader when Democrats take control of the Senate in January.
Democrats, for their part, are expected to keep their leaders. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, both of New York, are the favorites to become speaker and majority leader in January.
Jordan's pitch and his record point to the kind of minority he intends to lead. Democrats have said they plan to investigate the Pentagon's conduct of the Iran war, the dismissal of senior military officers and the military's strikes on suspected drug-smuggling boats once they hold the gavels. Jordan built his standing in the conference through oversight fights when Republicans were in the minority and through investigations when they were in the majority, and he told colleagues that experience was the reason to choose him. Scalise offered unity; the conference chose the candidate who promised a fight, by a margin of 33 votes.
His first test came the same evening. The House voted 211-204 to refer a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, filed by Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Republican, to the Judiciary Committee, which Jordan chairs. The vote ended the effort for this Congress without a recorded vote on the charges. Massie was the only Republican to side with Democrats.
The rest of the House Republican leadership slate had not been confirmed by Tuesday evening. Jordan takes over a conference that held together on its first hard vote of the lame-duck session, and that will spend the next two years on the receiving end of the kind of investigations he once led.

sources.news_title: What the House GOP’s Jim Jordan pick means for the direction of party
sources.text:
(CNN) — House Republicans are still reeling after the midterm elections decimated their ranks and set off a fight for the party’s future. Now, Jim Jordan, a pro-Trump, hardline conservative, will lead the party in the minority next year.
A dejected House GOP conference on Tuesday elected Jordan minority leader for the new Congress. The choice to elevate one of the GOP’s most combative figures signals Republicans are ready for all-out battle against Democrats in 2027.
Jordan, chairman of the Judiciary Committee, pitched himself to colleagues as the best-equipped to tee off an insurgent Democratic Party, which will have a robust oversight agenda targeting President Donald Trump’s White House. He’s also a high-octane former wrestling coach, with the ability to act as a political attack dog in a way that his allies said his challenger, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, lacks.
The Ohio lawmaker’s ascension is a rejection of the status quo that many Republicans believe cost them the election — by choosing not to promote their current No. 2 House Republican, Scalise. A veteran of House GOP leadership, Scalise is a more reserved, old-school conservative who famously survived a gunshot wound nearly a decade ago and is friendly with Trump.
But Republicans’ decision to back Jordan — who made a name for himself as a Freedom Caucus rebel and has long been one of Trump’s most stalwart defenders — is a reflection that Trump remains the party’s future, at least for now.
Rather than a path of moderation, the party is opting for a more hardline leader as it seeks relevance in the next two years. (The House GOP itself will also be a far more conservative group next year, with most of its remaining moderates wiped out, from New Jersey to Arizona, in the midterms.)
“[Trump] is still the leader of our party. We are going to be fighting tooth and nail to make sure his agenda continues to stay implemented,” a person familiar with his Jordan’s thinking told CNN.
Scalise had told members he would seek out ways to work with Democrats to achieve GOP priorities. But the person close to Jordan countered that Democrats had no reason to work with Republicans: “They have the numbers, they don’t need us. We need to be uniting as a team.”

Rep. Jim Jordan elected next House Republican leader after midterms blowout
See more of our coverage in your search results.
WASHINGTON — It’s Jordan time.
House Judiciary Committee chairman Jim Jordan won the right to lead Republicans in the lower chamber beginning next year as they brace for a massive incoming Democratic majority.
Jordan (R-Ohio) beat out House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) for the role after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) announced he wasn’t seeking the minority leader position in the next Congress.
The victory comes roughly eight years after the former assistant wrestling coach at The Ohio State University first launched a bid to become the top House Republican honcho, and marks his third attempt at landing the role. Jordan won in a 106-73 vote.
House Republicans also voted to keep Rep. Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) as their whip in the next Congress, who batted down a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), the head of the Republican Study Committee.
Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) also fended off a spirited challenge from Reps. Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) and Greg Steube (R-Fla.) for House GOP Conference chair.
On the other side of the Capitol, Senate Republicans tapped John Thune for a second two-year term as conference leader Tuesday following a contentious hours-long meeting.
The selection of Jordan, who co-founded and served as the inaugural chairman of House Freedom Caucus, a group of the most conservative lawmakers in the lower chamber, indicates that House Republicans plan to play hardball against the incoming Democratic majority.
“Congratulations to Jim Jordan,” House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris (R-Md.) said in a statement afterward. “A fierce fighter, uniter, principled conservative, and relentless advocate for the American people. Jim is exactly the right man for the job to fight back against the radical, crazy agenda of Democrats.”
Scalise, the current No. 2 House Republican, and Jordan previously squared off against each other in 2023 after the ouster of former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), with neither man able to claim the gavel. Scalise had edged Jordan out in that fight.
The Ohioan also vied to be minority leader in 2018 but lost that to McCarthy.
Both Jordan and Scalise acknowledged the daunting task Republicans face in reclaiming the House after facing one of the largest midterm wipeouts since the Watergate era, as well as the onslaught Democrats will soon mount against the Trump administration.
Scalise had pitched himself as a battle-tested leader with a “proven track record” in his outreach to Republicans. The Louisianan had been in a top four House GOP leadership position since 2014, when he was majority whip.
Meanwhile, Jordan billed himself as a scrappy outsider and highlighted his track record of being aggressive on the Judiciary panel while vowing to take Republicans on offense.
“I am battle-tested on the oversight front, and I know the Democrats’ playbook,” Jordan wrote in a letter to colleagues last week. “I know what it will take to lead our Conference in the minority, to stay unified, and to coordinate and calibrate our response to the Democrats’ tactics.”
“We need a Leadership team that is active and engaged, forward-thinking and straight-shooting.”
Both President Trump and Johnson stayed out of the House leadership contest. Johnson, who will lead Republicans for the rest of the year, has been coy about whether he plans to continue serving in Congress, despite winning reelection for another term.
Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) was one of the rare ex-speakers in recent decades who decided to stick around after losing the speakership.
“I’m encouraging the conference to unite around them [the new leaders] quickly. We have a lot of important work to do to wrap up this Congress and to finish strong,” Johnson told reporters.

House Republicans elected Republican Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan Tuesday to become the new party’s leader after Speaker Mike Johnson stepped aside.
Jordan ran against House Majority Leader Steve Scalise to become the next minority leader in the 120th Congress. Both Jordan and Scalise campaigned on fighting Democrats who are expected to launch investigations into President Donald Trump rather than focusing on tackling the cost of living, high gas prices and government corruption.
“We can expect Democrat legislation to wreak havoc on every sector of our economy and transform time-tested American institutions,” Jordan said in a Nov. 4 “Deal Colleague” letter. “Meanwhile, Democrats have already signaled their true intentions. Each Democrat-led committee will turn its full attention to investigating every facet of the Administration and private entities across the country.”
Scalise also warned his colleagues that Democrats planned to “unleash the most radical ‘oversight’ agenda we have seen in years.”
“House Democrats are about to unleash the most radical ‘oversight’ agenda we have seen in years. Yes, they will seek to impeach President Trump, but their focus will extend far beyond the Oval Office. They have made clear they will undertake a comprehensive approach that will target President Trump’s family, key cabinet officials, and any ally who has supported our America First agenda, including outside conservative partners and industry leaders,” Scalise continued. “Make no mistake: they will weaponize every single gavel.”
Voters handed Democrats major wins during the midterm elections as they soured on Trump’s handling of the cost of living and the Iran war. Twenty-seven percent of young people believe they are in a worse financial situation than their parents, particularly while the typical median age for a first-time home buyer in the U.S. is 40 years old, according to the Harvard Youth Poll from Oct. 22.
The average price of gas was $3.97 per gallon as of Tuesday, while Diesel prices were $6.15 per gallon, according to AAA. The average price was $3.07 per gallon in the previous year.
Members of the House Freedom Caucus and hardline Republicans backed Jordan, who co-founded the caucus alongside eight other Republicans. The caucus is made up of conservative lawmakers focused on advancing limited government, fiscal conservatism and populist policies.
Freedom Caucus members protested against House leadership’s votes during Johnson’s time as speaker. Members of the Freedom Caucus, including Republican Texas Rep. Chip Roy, voted against a rule in September to protest the passage of the continuing resolution (CR) particularly because it delayed a ban on hemp THC products.
Scalise is viewed as the more establishment candidate by comparison. He was elected as majority whip in 2014 and served as House minority whip from 2019 to 2022. He became House majority leader in 2023.
Jordan became chairman of the House Judiciary Committee in January 2023.
Scalise and Jordan ran for speaker after the House ousted former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in October 2023, although neither received the votes to assume the role. Scalise defeated Jordan by a vote of 113 to 99 on Oct. 11, 2023.

The race to lead House Republicans into the next Congress is starting to look a lot less like a coin flip — at least in the prediction markets.
Rep. Jim Jordan has emerged as the clear betting favorite over House Majority Leader Steve Scalise ahead of Tuesday’s closed-door leadership vote, giving the Ohio Republican a striking burst of momentum at the moment the conference is preparing for life in the minority.
When WLTReport checked Kalshi’s public election market shortly before noon Central, Jordan’s contract had last traded at 77 cents, with buyers bidding 74 cents and sellers asking 78 cents. Scalise’s contract had last traded at 24 cents, with a 22-to-26-cent spread.
That is a major gap. But it is not a vote count, and it should not be mistaken for one.
Prediction-market prices measure what traders believe is likely to happen. The only numbers that settle this race will come from Republican members and members-elect casting secret ballots behind closed doors.
Political reporter Reese Gorman described the contest Tuesday morning as a genuine toss-up inside the conference, even as the market moved sharply toward Jordan.

His pitch centers on aggressive oversight, tighter coordination, direct communication with voters, and a clearer set of policy alternatives. Jordan also pointed to his experience leading congressional investigations as preparation for the wave of Democrat-led probes expected in the next Congress.

Scalise is making a very different case. His letter to House Republicans emphasizes continuity, fundraising strength, legislative experience, and his long record of managing competing factions inside the conference.

Ohio Republican will take the lead after sweeping losses for Republicans
House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.
The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.
“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.
The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.
“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.
As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.
Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”
The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.
Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.
“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”
“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.
But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.
“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.
In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.
“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.
In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.
‘Tough choice’
But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.
Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.
Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”
Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.
Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.
“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”
Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.
The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.
“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

sources.news_title: House Republicans pick Jim Jordan as leader
sources.text:
House Republicans chose Jim Jordan on Tuesday to lead them in opposition to a Democratic-controlled Congress, according to a person familiar with the matter, putting a combative Donald Trump ally at the forefront of the party’s fight to defend the US president’s agenda during his final two years in office.
A secret ballot held behind closed doors elevated the Ohio Republican and House Judiciary Committee chairman to the minority leadership post a week after Democrats swept to victory in last Tuesday’s midterm elections, winning sizable majorities in both the House and Senate.
House Speaker Mike Johnson opted not to stand for the leadership position.
Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans met behind closed doors to decide whether to push forward with internal elections that were expected to retain US Senator John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, as the party leader or opt for a delay that could allow a challenger to emerge.
The House and Senate leadership elections will help determine what role Republicans intend to play as the minority party in Congress during the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Democrats will need Republican support to move major initiatives in the 100-member Senate, where the filibuster rule requires 60 votes for most legislation. Their majorities in both chambers also fall well short of the two-thirds votes needed to override presidential vetoes.
After the midterm elections, Thune vowed that Republicans would work with Trump to block “Democrat extremism” and work against any attempt by Democrats to unwind Republican achievements including border security and judicial appointments.
Jordan, 62, was first elected in 2006 to represent a deeply conservative rural district in northern Ohio and was a founder of the House Freedom Caucus, a group that former Republican Speaker John Boehner labeled “legislative terrorists”.

Club for Growth Congratulates Rep. Jim Jordan on Becoming House Minority Leader
Washington, D.C. – Club for Growth President David McIntosh issued the following statement after House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan (CFGF Lifetime Rating: 97%) Minority Leader for the 120th Congress. McIntosh previously endorsed Jordan for the position last week.
“We were proud to be with Jim Jordan in 2006, proud to join him in taking on the establishment, and proud to endorse him for Minority Leader. Club for Growth PAC was integral to his first primary victory, and nearly twenty years later he is still fighting for the same principles. His election is a great sign for the party, and the rest of the party should follow the direction House conservatives have chosen. We thank Speaker Johnson, another former Club for Growth PAC candidate, for his principled leadership and counsel.” – David McIntosh, President, Club for Growth.
